newsitem.title: USA: CBOT to list new delivery corn/soy futures Friday.
newsitem.headline: CBOT to list new delivery corn/soy futures Friday.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade said it will list four 1999 futures contracts for corn and soybeans on Friday that will be subject to proposed changes for Illinois River and Chicago-area delivery against futures.

The proposed changes have yet to be approved by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which said earlier on Thursday it would extend until June 16 the public comment period for the controversial plan.

"The CBOT will list the contracts with an asterisk to indicate the CBOT's Board of Directors and its membership have approved the terms of the contracts and that the terms are subject to CFTC approval," the CBOT said in a statement.

A CBOT spokesman said the exchange was listing the contracts to establish the normal forward positions for CBOT grains, but it distributed a circular to members warning that delivery terms might be subject to change, depending on the CFTC.

"We're listing these under the terms we've proposed to the CFTC. We have every reason to believe they will be approved. If the terms are not approved and there are no amendments or common agreement, then delivery would be under the terms that exist today," the CBOT spokesman said.
The CBOT has notified the CFTC of its listing plan, he said.
The contracts due for listing are July and November 1999 soybeans and July and December 1999 corn.

The CFTC's 60-day extension of public comment on the CBOT proposals came after widespread debate in the grain industry and among exchange members before CBOT members approved the changes on April 15 by a vote of 423-2/6 to 211-2/6.

Last December, CFTC said changes in grain marketing channels and shrinking Chicago-area elevator space meant the exchange must modify the delivery terms of the two contracts to prevent possible manipulation during delivery periods.
The CBOT plan eliminates Toledo as a delivery point and limits delivery sites to qualified elevators in Burns Harbor, Indiana, and between Chicago and Pekin on the Illinois River.
CFTC chairwoman Brooksley Born said on March 31 the agency hoped to act quickly on the CBOT plan.

But the proposals drew more than 250 comments from politicans, grain cooperatives and farmers during the CFTC's first comment period. Most said they opposed the changes and urged the agency to consider other options.
